notes.meaning: Samuel died, and all the people of Israel gathered to weep for him and bury him at his home in Ramah. Samuel had served God faithfully as a prophet and righteous leader for many decades. After the funeral, David moved further south into the wilderness of Paran to find safety.

A very wealthy man lived in the town of Maon and ran his livestock business nearby in Carmel. He owned three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. At this time, he was shearing his sheep, which was always a season of celebration and great feasting.

The man was named Nabal, which means fool, and he lived up to his name by being crude, stubborn, and mean. In contrast, his wife Abigail was both sensible and beautiful. Nabal came from the noble family line of Caleb, but he showed none of his ancestor's good character.

While David and his men were living out in the wilderness, they heard that Nabal was shearing his flocks. Because sheep-shearing brought rich feasts and plenty of food, David knew it was a good time to ask for supplies. He hoped Nabal would be in a generous mood.

David chose ten of his young men and sent them up to Carmel to meet Nabal. He told them to give Nabal a warm and respectful greeting in his name. Sending a group of ten messengers showed honor and courtesy toward a wealthy neighbor.

David told his messengers to bless Nabal with long life and prosperity. They were to speak peace over Nabal, his family, and everything he owned. David wanted to begin their meeting with kindness and goodwill.

David reminded Nabal that his men had stayed close to Nabal's shepherds in the countryside. David's soldiers had never harmed the shepherds or stolen a single animal. In an untamed wilderness, this kind of protection from an armed band was a rare and valuable blessing.

David invited Nabal to ask his own workers, who would gladly confirm the report. Since David's men had arrived on a festive day of celebration, David asked Nabal to share whatever extra food he had on hand. He even called himself Nabal's son, showing deep respect to an older man.
David’s messengers reached Carmel and spoke every word to Nabal just as David had ordered. Once they finished their respectful request, they sat down quietly and waited for his answer.

Nabal replied with sharp insults, pretending he had never heard of David or the son of Jesse. He mocked David as nothing more than a runaway servant fleeing from his master, King Saul. Nabal used these cruel words to cover up his own greed.

Nabal refused to give away his bread, water, or meat prepared for his workers. He claimed he had no reason to feed wandering men whose origins he did not know. Water and meat were valuable in that dry country, and Nabal selfishly hoarded everything for himself.
David’s young men did not yell back or start a fight. They turned around, walked back to their camp in the wilderness, and told David everything Nabal had said.

When David heard the insults, he lost his temper and commanded his men to strap on their swords. About four hundred armed men marched out with David to take revenge, while two hundred stayed behind to guard their gear. David reacted in fierce anger rather than asking God what he should do.

One of Nabal’s shepherds hurried to warn Abigail about what had happened. He told her that David had sent messengers out of the desert to greet their master kindly, but Nabal had screamed at them with rage. The servant saw that this terrible insult would bring disaster.

The servant explained that David’s men had been remarkably kind to the shepherds in the open fields. David's soldiers had never mistreated them, and not a single sheep had gone missing while they were camped nearby. The servant gave clear proof of David's good conduct.

David’s men had served as a protective wall around Nabal's shepherds day and night. They had kept the flocks safe from wild animals and roaming desert bandits. Without that steady shield, Nabal would have suffered heavy losses.

The servant pleaded with Abigail to think fast and take action, because total ruin was coming for Nabal and everyone in his home. He warned that Nabal was such a worthless scoundrel that no one could even talk to him. The servant knew only Abigail had the wisdom to save them.

Abigail moved quickly to gather a large feast for David and his men. She packed two hundred loaves of bread, two large leather skins of wine, five cooked sheep, roasted grain, raisin cakes, and pressed fig cakes onto donkeys. Having so much food on hand showed just how wealthy Nabal really was.

Abigail told her servants to ride ahead with the supplies, promising she would follow right behind them. She did not tell her husband Nabal anything about her plan. She knew his stubborn pride would stop her and bring about the death of the whole family.

As Abigail rode her donkey down into a hidden mountain ravine, David and his soldiers were marching down the opposite side. Suddenly, they met each other in the valley between the hills. God guided their steps so they met before any fighting began.

Just before meeting Abigail, David had been talking to himself and his men in fierce anger. He complained that guarding Nabal's goods in the desert had been a waste of time, since Nabal had repaid his kindness with evil. David let his wounded pride drive his thoughts.

David swore a reckless oath, promising that God should punish him severely if he left a single male in Nabal's house alive by morning. Instead of cursing his own name directly, he spoke of God punishing his enemies. This rash vow showed how uncontrolled rage can lead even a faithful servant of God toward murder.
